tool_calls.arguments: {"summary":"Putting ₱10,000 a month on the card and the rest into the emergency fund pays the card in 7 months and gets the emergency fund to its target in 4 months; it also cuts credit-card interest to ₱9,358.80 (debt1-W1). tool_calls.name: ask_debt
tool_calls.arguments: {"question": "This is a replan after Mara's new job was approved from Dec 1, 2026. Please compare two card-focused moves Jun asked about: ₱10,000 a month on the credit card with the rest in the emergency fund, versus all unallocated surplus on the credit card, keeping the household's avalanche strategy and flexibility preference in view and revisiting Decisions D1 to D3."}

tool_calls.arguments: {"question": "This is a replan after Mara's new job was approved from Dec 1, 2026. Please assess the emergency fund under Jun's two choices: ₱10,000 a month on the credit card with the rest in the emergency fund, versus all unallocated surplus on the credit card, and revisit Decisions D1 to D3 because Mara's salary changed."}

tool_calls.name: submit_answer
tool_calls.arguments:
{"reply":"Yes — Mara’s new job gives you more room each month, so this replan is mainly a choice between faster credit-card payoff and a stronger cash buffer.

If you want to stay close to your earlier choices, the split option matches them best: it puts ₱10,000.00 a month on the card and the rest into the emergency fund. That gets the emergency fund to target in 4 months and clears the card in 7 months.

If you want the fastest debt push, the all-on-card option pays the card sooner and lowers interest more, but it leaves the emergency fund with no new monthly allocation for now.

What I’d weigh: your approved preference is flexibility, and your earlier decisions also leaned toward keeping more cash on hand while Lia starts school and while you wanted a bigger buffer. That points more toward the split. But if your priority now is to finish the card as fast as possible, the all-on-card option does that.","options":[{"label":"A: split between the card and emergency fund","what_if":"rec-W1","summary":"Put ₱10,000.00 a month on the credit card and ₱15,050.00 a month into the emergency fund. Those decisions should be revisited because Mara’s salary changed, but they still point more toward building the emergency fund while paying the credit card down."}
